title: Earth Is Made of Rock
keyIdea: The ground under your feet is rock. If you dig down through the soil, you always reach solid rock. Rock is all around us: mountains, cliffs, pebbles and even sand are rock. Big rocks slowly break into stones, pebbles and tiny grains of sand. Some rocks are hard and some are soft, like chalk, but they are all rock. The outside of Earth is rock all the way round, under the land and under the sea.
familyTip: Go on a rock hunt in a park, a beach or your street. Pick up a pebble, feel some sand and look at a wall or a step. For each one, ask: is this a bit of the Earth? Rub two pebbles together over paper and look at the tiny grains that fall off.

visual.caption: Is it rock? Drag each card, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: dig down to solid rock, find rock in a landscape, break a boulder into sand, sort rocks, and drill under a city and the sea.

kid: The ground under your feet is rock. On top there is grass and soil. Plants grow in the soil. If you dig down and down, you hit hard, solid rock.
You can see rock in lots of places. A mountain is a huge pile of rock. A cliff is a wall of rock. Pebbles are small rocks. Sand is tiny bits of rock.
Big rocks break into small bits. Rain, ice and waves wear them away. It takes a very long time. A big rock turns into stones, then pebbles, then sand.
Some rocks are hard. Some are soft, like chalk. They are all rock. Earth is like a giant ball. Its outside is rock all the way round, even under the sea.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. The idea that Earth is made of rock and other natural materials underpins the rocks units of the National Curriculum in England (Year 2 everyday materials, Year 3 rocks and soils) and NGSS 2-ESS1-1 and 4-ESS2-1 on slow changes and weathering by water, ice and wind. Children learn that soil is a thin top layer made partly of broken rock, that solid rock (bedrock) lies under it everywhere, and that sand and pebbles are pieces of rock.

The lab has five tasks. Children dig a hole through soil and stony soil to bedrock, find the rock in a landscape (mountain, cliff, beach sand, river pebbles) while a tree and a cloud are not, break a boulder into stones, pebbles and sand, sort seven cards into rock and not rock, and drill under a city, the sea and a desert. The outer layer of Earth, the crust, is solid rock all the way round, including under the oceans.

Common mistakes. Many children think soil goes down forever, that Earth is hollow, or that rocks must be hard, so they reject chalk and sand. Some think pebbles grow or are made by people. Take care with the deep Earth: the mantle is very hot rock and the outer core is liquid metal, so this lesson says the outside of Earth is rock, not that Earth is rock all the way to the centre.

practice.prompt: You dig a deep hole in the garden. What do you reach under the soil?
practice.hint: Think about what the spade hit at the bottom of the hole in the lab.
practice.explain: Under the soil there is always solid rock. Soil is only a thin top layer.

practice.prompt: You find {a} pebbles and {b} shells on the beach. How many pebbles are pieces of rock?
practice.hint: Pebbles are rock. Shells were made by sea animals, so do not count them.
practice.explain: All {a} pebbles are rock. The {b} shells are not rock, so the answer is {a}.

practice.hint: Waves grind pebbles smaller and smaller. What is left?
practice.explain: Sand is tiny grains of rock. Waves and wind wear big rocks down into sand.

practice.prompt: A big rock breaks into {n} stones. Then one stone breaks in 2. How many pieces now?
practice.hint: One stone turns into 2, so you have one more piece than before.
practice.explain: {n} stones, and one splits in 2, makes {=n+1} pieces. They are all still rock.

practice.prompt: Chalk is soft. Is chalk a rock?
practice.hint: In the lab, where did the chalk card go?
practice.explain: Chalk is a soft rock. Some rocks are hard and some are soft, but they are all rock.

pool.prompt: Which of these is made of rock?
pool.hint: One of them grows and one floats in the sky.
pool.explain: A mountain is a huge pile of rock. A tree is a living plant and a cloud is water drops.

pool.hint: Think about the boulder you broke in the lab.
pool.explain: Pebbles are bits of bigger rocks. Rivers and waves roll them until they are smooth.

pool.prompt: Sam has {a} pebbles. He finds {b} more on a path. How many rocks does he have now?
pool.hint: Pebbles are small rocks, so add them all.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} pebbles, and every pebble is a rock.

pool.prompt: What is under the sea floor?
pool.hint: Remember the drill under the sea in the lab.
pool.explain: The outside of Earth is rock all the way round, under the land and under the sea.

pool.prompt: Mia says rocks must be hard. What do you say?
choices: Some rocks are soft, like chalk
pool.hint: Think of a soft rock that you can draw with.
pool.explain: Most rocks are hard, but chalk is a soft rock. Hard or soft, it is still rock.

pool.prompt: You dig {n} spades of soil, then hit rock. You dig 1 more spade. How many spades in all?
pool.hint: Add the 1 extra spade to the spades of soil.
pool.explain: {n} + 1 = {=n+1} spades. Under the soil, the spade always hits rock.

pool.prompt: Which of these is not rock?
pool.hint: One of them grew on a tree.
pool.explain: A leaf grew on a tree, so it is not rock. Pebbles and sand are bits of rock.

pool.prompt: What turns big rocks into sand?
choices: Rain, ice and waves, over a long time
People with hammers, in one day
pool.hint: The lab said this takes many, many years.
pool.explain: Rain, ice, rivers and waves wear rock away very slowly. In time, big rocks become sand.
